Read `README.md` and current rollout evidence first. Produce exactly one multi-wake target-policy candidate in `solver/`. Keep candidate-specific reasoning in `logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md`, and add or materially revise at least one evidence-backed reusable lesson in `guidance/control_experience.md` from the assigned parent, sampled solver results, and inherited logs. If no positive lesson survives the evidence, record a concrete negative result and what later workers should avoid or test. The candidate is incomplete until both files are updated. Work only inside this Phase 2 workspace.

Use the fish-control bookshelf through this structured transfer protocol:

1. Before the first architecture proposal from the common naive seed, consult `guidance/skills/fish-control-primitives/SKILL.md` and its references.
2. On later iterations, consult it again when the inherited guidance indicates three consecutive completed iterations with neither a new controller mechanism nor a semantic improvement such as a new success, a better termination class, or a meaningfully different useful trajectory.
3. Consultation is required at those moments; adopting a primitive is optional. Do not use the shelf to justify scalar-only gain tuning.
4. If a source informs the edit, record a concise block in `logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md`:

```text
bookshelf_consulted: true
source_domain:
source_mechanism:
transferable_invariant:
nontransferable_details:
policy_translation:
falsification:
```

Translate only the invariant into normalized body-frame observations and the two-joint state-feedback contract. Prefer one mechanism or one small compatible combination. Published gains, species-specific kinematics, exact vortex phases, and task-specific routes are not transferable answers.

I’ll first establish the Phase 2 contract from `README.md`, then inspect the inherited rollout evidence and both wake visual views before touching the candidate. I’ll also apply the required fish-control bookshelf protocol and keep the candidate-specific rationale separate from the reusable guidance.

`README.md` confirms a single editable policy file, mandatory pre-edit notes, a durable guidance revision, no local CFD, and a final policy-contract check. I’m now reading the inherited guidance plus the two required skill protocols; the visual protocol will determine which rollout views must be inspected before I form the architecture hypothesis.

The inherited bank shows the current branch has already exhausted many scalar/gating tweaks. The strongest semantic change is the bounded target-radial carrier reserve (`23.375T` capture), while one-sided speed projection and several terminal signal substitutions regressed. I’ll now inspect all four sampled artifacts, explicitly comparing the faster carrier example against an informative failed/regressed mechanism, and will not propose the new mechanism until after that evidence and the bookshelf references are read.

The compact diagnostics confirm all four are valid direct-uniform still-water captures, so “failure” here means a regressed controller mechanism rather than failed termination. The assigned parent’s demand-handoff policy is strongest (`23.3750T`, mean `2.40075L`, score `-0.503415`); the middle-handoff re-engagement is the most informative regression (`23.4355T`, mean `2.40196L`) because it directly tests where the extra propulsion is applied. I’m visually comparing those two from release through capture in both rows now.

The wake sheets agree with the metrics: both policies are self-propelled along the same gently curved route, shed an orderly alternating top-down street, and retain compact three-dimensional Lambda2 structures through capture; the middle re-engagement changes timing/terminal approach more than wake topology. That makes the remaining defect a carrier–terminal-control coordination problem, not a missing-wake problem.

This is the mandated bookshelf consultation point. I’m reading its mechanism catalog and source notes now; if one invariant survives the rollout evidence, I’ll translate only that invariant into the normalized body-frame, two-joint feedback contract and record the required provenance block.

The shelf contributes one compatible invariant: preserve the traveling carrier and change authority asymmetrically by observed beat side, rather than weakening the whole gait. I’m adopting that as a terminal half-cycle cadence handoff: keep the evaluated target-progress reserve unchanged before `3L`, but withdraw only the extra reserve on the observed tail-bend half-cycle that supports carrier-rejected excess yaw. The base cadence, route steering, split observer, posterior lag/amplitude, and command projection stay intact.

This is a genuinely new state-feedback mechanism, not a gain retune. Its decisive test is whether it preserves the current `23.375T` progress while improving the `1–2L` yaw/moment tradeoff; the inherited evidence says whole-cycle withdrawal loses closing speed. I’m recording that hypothesis and the bookshelf transfer block before editing, as required by both skills.

The policy now contains exactly one new mechanism: a continuous, observed half-cycle handoff of only the small target-progress cadence reserve. No gain was added, and the existing two-joint carrier/steering architecture remains otherwise unchanged.

I’m now folding the four sampled handoff results into the durable experience bank. The reusable lesson is sharper than “reduce terminal cadence”: all samples share the same pre-`3L` trajectory and coherent wake, while whole-cycle relief trades away final closing and demand-gated relief leaves a mixed moment/cross-track defect. That bounds future work to phase-localized relief unless new CFD shows a different trajectory regime.

Both required files are now materially updated. Before invoking the mandated checker, I’m doing a quick local contract audit: one non-empty candidate, every `params.FIELD` declared, no forbidden clocks/global routes, and a focused diff against the assigned parent. Then I’ll hand the finished workspace to the configured check-runner and repair any reported failure without running CFD.

The configured check-runner was invoked, but its pinned `gpt-5.4-mini` runtime is unavailable on this account, so it could not start. I’m not treating that infrastructure error as validation; I’m running the exact three commands from its TOML separately here, with the same no-CFD scope.

The semantic-guidance check and repository boundary check pass. The lightweight Julia command is blocked by the environment (`julia: command not found`), not by a policy assertion. I’m checking for any bundled Julia runtime; if none exists, I’ll run the deterministic schema/forbidden-state guards directly and report the one unavailable runtime check explicitly.

The direct static audit passes: there is one non-empty candidate, all 69 referenced parameter fields are declared, and the edit introduces no elapsed time, step counter, randomness, file I/O, or mutable global state. The unavailable Julia executable is the only check limitation; the policy delta is syntactically small and sits on an already evaluated parent.

I’ve also documented that this workspace contained no inherited optimizer-log artifact, so the provenance accurately distinguishes the available parent, sampled rollouts, and guidance examples. I’m rerunning the semantic check after that final note update and collecting the final hashes/locations.

Produced exactly one Phase 2 candidate: a state-feedback half-cycle handoff that withdraws only the extra target-progress cadence reserve during excess-yaw-supporting bends.
